🚀 Welcome to AgroOrbit Nexus! 🌱🛰️

We are building an innovative AI-powered web platform that uses NASA Earth observation data to help farmers make smarter, more sustainable crop rotation decisions.

Our goal is to combine artificial intelligence, climate science, and modern web technologies to create a real-world impact.

We're looking for passionate teammates interested in AI, software development, data science, UX/UI design, and agriculture.
summary:
AgroOrbit Nexus — From Space to Soil is an interactive, bilingual web platform designed to help farmers and agricultural advisors make better crop rotation decisions using NASA Earth observation data.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, our solution addresses the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge by transforming NASA POWER climate data into understandable comparisons of agricultural strategies.

The platform combines NASA climate observations with FAO-56 methodologies to estimate crop water demand, evaluate soil-health indicators, and explore the effects of historical El Niño conditions. Users can compare crop rotations, adjust their priorities, visualize results, and export evidence-based reports.

In our pilot case in Virú, Peru, an alternative crop rotation demonstrated approximately 1,390 m³/ha lower modeled water demand than continuous maize cultivation.

AgroOrbit Nexus bridges the gap between space technology and everyday farming, making scientific data more accessible while supporting sustainable agriculture, efficient water management, and climate resilience. Results are exploratory and require local agronomic validation.
details:
AgroOrbit Nexus — From Space to Soil

1. Project Overview

AgroOrbit Nexus is an interactive, bilingual agricultural decision-support platform that transforms NASA Earth observation data into understandable insights for farmers and agricultural extension agents.

Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data," by helping users explore how different crop rotation strategies may affect agricultural water demand, soil-health indicators, and climate resilience.

Instead of presenting a single crop recommendation, AgroOrbit Nexus allows users to compare multiple agricultural scenarios, understand the reasoning behind their results, and make more informed decisions before planting.

2. How Does It Work?

The platform follows five main steps:

Step 1 — Select a location: Users can search for a location, use their current position, or select an area on an interactive map. The application identifies the corresponding NASA POWER climate-data grid and explains its spatial resolution.

Step 2 — Define crop rotations: Users enter their crop history, planned rotation, and up to two alternative strategies.

Step 3 — Analyze NASA climate data: The application retrieves daily temperature and precipitation observations from NASA POWER. Using FAO-56 methods, including the Hargreaves reference evapotranspiration equation and crop coefficients, it estimates crop water demand.

Step 4 — Compare agricultural strategies: Users can analyze water demand, crop diversity, legume inclusion, repeated planting, uncropped periods, and historical El Niño climate scenarios. Adjustable priority sliders allow farmers to explore trade-offs between water conservation, soil-health indicators, and crop diversification.

Step 5 — Export results: The application provides interactive comparisons, transparent scoring explanations, printable reports, and JSON exports containing the data, assumptions, and calculation rules.

3. Results and Benefits

Our initial case study focuses on Virú, Peru, where efficient irrigation management is particularly important.

Using real NASA POWER climate data, AgroOrbit Nexus compares three illustrative crop rotation strategies:

  • Continuous maize cultivation: approximately 13,120 m³/ha of modeled crop water demand.
  • Maize–bean–maize rotation: approximately 12,720 m³/ha.
  • Maize–sorghum–bean rotation: approximately 11,730 m³/ha.

The third strategy demonstrates approximately 1,390 m³/ha less modeled water demand than continuous maize cultivation while introducing greater crop diversity and interrupting repeated maize planting.

These results represent a modeled comparison, not measured water savings or field-validated recommendations.

4. Technologies and Tools Used

AgroOrbit Nexus was developed using modern web technologies and scientific methodologies:

  • NASA POWER API: Real Earth observation-based climate data.
  • FAO-56 methodologies: Reference evapotranspiration and crop water-demand estimation.
  • Next.js 16 and React 19: Interactive web application.
  • TypeScript: Application logic, calculations, and data processing.
  • Tailwind CSS: Responsive interface design.
  • MapLibre: Interactive geographical exploration.
  • Recharts: Climate and agricultural data visualizations.
  • Zod: Data validation.
  • Vitest, Playwright, and axe: Automated testing and accessibility checks.
  • GitHub and Vercel: Source-code management and web deployment.

The platform is available in English and Spanish and works directly through a web browser without requiring specialized hardware.

5. Innovation and Creativity

AgroOrbit Nexus connects space-based climate observations with practical agricultural decision-making.

Its main innovation is combining transparent scientific calculations, interactive crop rotation comparisons, historical climate stress tests, and farmer-defined priorities within a single accessible platform.

Unlike systems that provide unexplained recommendations, AgroOrbit Nexus makes its assumptions, calculations, limitations, and comparison criteria visible to users.

The platform also distinguishes between satellite-derived climate information and local field conditions, helping users understand what the available data can and cannot establish.

6. Intended Impact

Our goal is to make NASA Earth observation data more accessible and useful for agricultural communities, particularly in regions facing water scarcity and climate variability.

AgroOrbit Nexus aims to support:

  • More informed crop rotation planning.
  • Greater awareness of agricultural water demand.
  • Exploration of crop diversification and soil-health practices.
  • Better understanding of historical climate risks.
  • Accessible, evidence-based discussions between farmers and agricultural advisors.

Although the platform can access climate information worldwide, agronomic comparisons depend on the availability of regional crop profiles. Our initial demonstration focuses on Virú, Peru.

Future development could incorporate additional local crop profiles, field measurements, and validation with agronomists and farming communities.

7. Scientific Responsibility

The project uses documented scientific methods and openly communicates its limitations.

Water-demand estimates are based on NASA climate observations and generic FAO-56 crop coefficients. Soil-health indicators are derived from crop rotation characteristics rather than direct soil measurements.

The current prototype has not undergone regional field validation and does not claim measured irrigation savings, yield improvements, or guaranteed agricultural outcomes.

Our objective is to provide an understandable, reproducible exploration tool that helps bridge the gap between satellite science and sustainable agriculture.
